# Introduction 

The data comes from [Banking Dataset - Marketing Targets](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/prakharrathi25/banking-dataset-marketing-targets). This is picked up from publicly available research data [UCI Machine Learning](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Bank+Marketing) using random sampling plus a few additional columns are introduced in Kaggle data.

In Project 2, I explored this data with an interactive Shiny app. The goal of this (final) project is to predict **`y`**
y is a categorical outcome of the campaign, therefore we will be working on a binary classification problem. 

**Client Traits (column names in the data set):**

## bank client data:

1.  age (numeric)
2.  job : type of job (categorical: "admin.","unknown","unemployed","management","housemaid","entrepreneur","student","blue-collar","self-employed","retired","technician","services")
3.  marital : marital status (categorical: "married","divorced","single"; note: "divorced" means divorced or widowed)
4.  education (categorical: "unknown","secondary","primary","tertiary")
5.  default: has credit in default? (binary: "yes","no")
6.  balance: average yearly balance, in euros (numeric)
7.  housing: has housing loan? (binary: "yes","no")
8.  loan: has personal loan? (binary: "yes","no") 

## related with the last contact of the current campaign:

9.  contact: contact communication type (categorical: "unknown","telephone","cellular")
10. day: last contact day of the month (numeric)
11. month: last contact month of year (categorical: "jan", "feb", "mar", …, "nov", "dec")
12. duration: last contact duration, in seconds (numeric) 

## other attributes:

13. campaign: number of contacts performed during this campaign and for this client (numeric, includes last contact)
14. pdays: number of days that passed by after the client was last contacted from a previous campaign (numeric, -1. means client was not previously contacted)
15. previous: number of contacts performed before this campaign and for this client (numeric)
16. poutcome: outcome of the previous marketing campaign (categorical: "unknown","other","failure","success")

**Output variable (desired target):**

1.  y - has the client subscribed a term deposit? (binary: "yes","no")

# Setup

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(rpart.plot)
```


# Read the data 

As shown in Project 2, `test.csv` is just a 10% random sample of `train.csv`, so `train.csv` along holds all clients.

```{r}
bank_raw <- read_delim("data/train.csv", delim = ";")
bank_raw
```

# Pre-processing
First, let's check for missing values and for the string `"unknown"` -- which is showong up in contact and poutcome columns 

```{r}
colSums(is.na(bank_raw))
colSums(bank_raw == "unknown")
```

No columns contain `NA` values
But 4 different columns with vast number of observations contain unknnown so let's make `"unknown"` its own level. 

Let's now make categorical columns factors.

```{r}
bank_all <- bank_raw |>
  mutate(
    across(where(is.character), as.factor)
  )
str(bank_all)
levels(bank_all$y)
```

# Exploratory Data Analysis 

## Outcome - y

```{r}
table(bank_all$y)

```

## Categorical Predictors vs y

### housing vs y


```{r}
bank_all |>
  count(housing, y) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = y, values_from = n) |>
  mutate(rate = yes / (yes+no))


```

Housing categorical variable is showing some varition on the outcome. People with no housing cost seem to be able to subscribe at higher rate. We will be including this as a categorical predictor. 

### poutcome vs y

```{r}
bank_all |>
  count(poutcome, y) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = y, values_from = n) |>
  mutate(rate = yes / (yes+no))


```
It appears, past-outcome is influencing current outcome. If the poutcome is success there is ~65% of chance of resubscribing. Similarly if poutcome is failure then the rate is 12%. This is definitely a useful predictor to be included for this project. 


## Numerical Predictors vs y

Let's explore some numerical predicators now

### age vs y
there is some evidence that job and education are directly related to age. So checking age first (also just including age and not job education will help us reduce multicollinearity)

```{r}
bank_all |>
  mutate(age_group = case_when(
    age <= 25 ~ "25 and under",
    age <= 30 ~ "26 to 30",
    age <= 40 ~ "31 to 40",
     age <= 50 ~ "41 to 50",
     age <= 60 ~ "51 to 60",
    age > 60 ~ "over 60"
  )) |>
  count(age_group , y) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = y, values_from = n) |>
  mutate(total = yes + no,
         rate = yes /total)
```

In the table above every row has more than 1000 clients. As we can see the subscription rate was about 24% under 25 and then dropped until age 50. Then it climbed to 42% after age 60. Thefore age seems be significantly contributing to the outcome.

Let's split this further and show under 17 and 18-25

```{r}
bank_all |>
  mutate(age_group = case_when(
    age <= 17 ~ "17 and under",
    age <= 25 ~ "18 to 25",
    age <= 30 ~ "26 to 30",
    age <= 40 ~ "31 to 40",
     age <= 50 ~ "41 to 50",
     age <= 60 ~ "51 to 60",
    age > 60 ~ "over 60"
  )) |>
  count(age_group , y) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = y, values_from = n) |>
  mutate(total = yes + no,
         rate = yes /total)

```

That did not change the table. There were no clients under 18 

Checking the range of clients:

```{r}

range(bank_all$age)

```

bank_all |>

Subscribers have generally higher mean and median bank balances compared to the ones that did not subscribe.

Balance shows clear connection with output. Let's include balance as the predictor. 

### campaign vs y

Final Predictors before starting modeling

# Modeling

## Train/ test split 

Let's select the 5 predictor columns + response column and then do a 70-30 split on the data. Let's use response as strata so both train and test have same proportion of yes/no observations 

```{r}
set.seed(558)

bank <- bank_all |>
  select(y, housing, poutcome, age, balance, campaign)

bank_split <- initial_split(bank, prop = 0.7, strata = y)
bank_train <- training(bank_split)
bank_test <- testing(bank_split)

```

Let's check yes/no balance in both training and testing sets

```{r}

bank_train |> 
  count(y) |> 
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n))

bank_test |> 
  count(y) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n))

```

## Cross validation folds

Using 5 fold cross validation to select best model from each family of models:
- classification tree (not regression tree because the response is a categorical/class variable)
- random forest 

```{r}
bank_folds <- vfold_cv(bank_train, v = 5, strata = y)
bank_folds

```
There are 31,647 observations in the training data. 
5 fold CV splits them into 5 folds of about 6,330 observations each (or 6329 in some folds). In each of the 5 iterations, the model is fit on 4 folds (about 25,300 observations) and evaluated on the remaining fold which is the validation fold. Each fold serves as the validation fold exactly once. The log-loss is averaged for these 5 iterations. 

CV helps to select the hyperparameters that are not influenced by specific subset of training data. Instead all of the training data is used for both fitting and evaluatiing the model in different iterations and for each combination of the tuning-grid/hyperparameter selection 

The test set is not used in CV process. 


## Metric for selecting the best model from each family 

I will go with log-loss function. 
Basically in a classification problem we have to maximize the likelihood of correctly estimating the outcome which translates to minimizing negative likelihood function aka log-loss function. 
One other option considered is accuracy - however the share of subscribers is about 12%. Therefore, a model that learns to classify every customer as "no" gets it right 88% of the times which is not meaningful. An 88% accuracy would only be meaningful if the outcome classes were balanced. 



```{r}
bank_metrics <- metric_set(mn_log_loss)

```


# Classification tree 



A classification tree falls under the category of supervised learning models and isi used when the response variable is categorical.

The idea behind a tree-based model is to split the predictor space into different regions and make a prediction for reach region. Unlike logistic regression, the predictions in adjacent regions do not necessarily have to be close to each other.

One of the interesting things we noticed during our EDA was that the subscription rate went from approximately 10% to 42% around the age of 60. A tree-based model could potentially capture this pattern by splitting the data based on age.

## How does the model make predictions?

In a regression tree, as we saw in HW10, the prediction is the mean of a response variable in a given region. In a classification tree, however, the prediction is the most prevalent class in that region.

Since we are using log-loss as our metric, we are interested in the probability of a client subscribing to a term deposit. This probability can be obtained by looking at the proportion of clients who subscribed within a given terminal node.

## How does the tree fit?
 
The fitting is done by recursive binary splitting, which is greedy; it picks the best split that minimizes loss at each step without looking ahead. At each step it tries every predictor and every possible cut point, and chooses the split that makes the two new regions as close to all `yes` or all `no` as possible, then repeats this within each new region. 

## What is Pruning?

If we keep splitting, the tree will grow very large and overfit the training data. Trees are usually grown large first and then pruned back using cost-complexity pruning which is controlled by the `cost_complexity` tuning parameter.

## What are the other tuning parameters?

The other tuning parameter I use this `tree_depth`, which sets the maximum depth of the tree. The final tree is limited by the stricter of `cost_complexity` or `tree_depth`
Another parameter, `min_n`, is the minimum number of observations a node needs before it can split. I will leave it as  the default of 20. 

I tune `cost_complexity` and `tree_depth` together using a grid of 5 values each, which gives 25 combinations. Each combination is fit using the 5-fold CV described above, and the one with the lowest average log-loss is selected 


## Recipe 

Trees can handle factors directly and dont need the numeric predictors to be standardized.. The recipe only needs the formula

```{r}
bank_recipe <- recipe(y ~ ., data = bank_train)
bank_recipe

```

## Fitting the classificaiton tree

```{r}

tree_spec <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = tune(), tree_depth = tune()) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")


tree_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(bank_recipe) |>
  add_model(tree_spec)


tree_grid <- grid_regular(cost_complexity(), tree_depth(), levels = 5)

tree_results <- tree_workflow |>
  tune_grid(resamples = bank_folds, grid = tree_grid, metrics = bank_metrics)

# arrange the 25 trees by the mean value of mn_log_loss in ascending order 
collect_metrics(tree_results) |>
  arrange(mean)

```


## Best classification tree

```{r}

# Let's select the best tuning parameters -- which is pre0_mod17_post0 from above

tree_best_params <- select_best(tree_results, metric = "mn_log_loss")
tree_best_params

```

Now let's repalce `tune()` with best values 

```{r}
tree_final_workflow <- tree_workflow |>
  finalize_workflow(tree_best_params)


```

Now let's fit the full training data on the final winning tree model 

```{r}
tree_final_fit <- tree_final_workflow |>
  fit(bank_train)

```

Now let's plot to visualiize final tree

```{r}
tree_final_fit |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  rpart.plot(roundint = FALSE)

```
The tree splits on poutcome first. if the previous campaign was a scuess, about 65% of those clients subscribed, but the remaining 97% of clients all go into on leaf with only about 10% chance of subscribing. The success group gets split further by housing, campaign and balance, and clients with no housing loan and fewer calls have the highest rate at 71%. Interestingly, age is not usued anywhere in the tree even though it looked useful during the EDA.
